issues.description: Solution repository uses classes named SpaceSeal, SpacePig, and SpaceGoat while the problem statement and template expect Seal, Pig, and Goat. The solution also contains empty Goat.java, Pig.java, and Seal.java files. This naming/structural divergence can confuse students (they will implement Seal/Pig/Goat per the UML and template), and it may break comparisons or automated checks that expect the non-prefixed class names.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the solution with the exercise specification: provide concrete implementations named Seal, Pig, and Goat (matching the UML and template) or update the problem statement and template to consistently use the Space-prefixed class names. Ensure Goat.java, Pig.java, and Seal.java in the solution contain the intended implementations rather than being empty placeholders.

issues.description: The problem statement and the template refer to concrete animal classes named Seal, Pig, and Goat, but the solution implementation provides these animals under different identifiers (SpaceSeal, SpacePig, SpaceGoat). This inconsistency means students reading the exercise (which names Seal/Pig/Goat and shows them in UML) will not find corresponding implemented classes in the solution; the solution also contains empty placeholder files for Seal/Pig/Goat while actual implementations use the Space* prefixes. This creates unnecessary mapping confusion between the required class names in the task and the names used in the final implementation.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the class names across artifacts. Either rename the solution classes to Seal, Pig, and Goat (i.e., SpaceSeal -> Seal, SpacePig -> Pig, SpaceGoat -> Goat) or update the problem statement and template to explicitly use the Space-prefixed names. If the Space* naming is intentional, keep the expected class files (Seal/Pig/Goat) as thin wrappers or aliases that delegate to the Space* implementations so students can map the problem UML to concrete classes without confusion.
